docs.title: ETHRC Drone Racing
docs.text:
Page Owner: Members of the Aeronautics Division

Welcome to the ETHRC Drone Racing project documentation! The project is currently still in development and is not yet ready for public use. Still, we want to that as soon as we have reached our goals and are ready to release the project. This documentation is hence really important!

Everyone in the project is free to commit changes to the docs and we really encourage you to do so! If you are unsure whether the information belongs here or on our Notion page, then feel free to ask. Otherwise the answer to the question "If the repo goes public, would this be relevant to them?" should guide your decision. Generally anything technical (implementation details, technical decisions etc.) belong here.

Please note that some pages have a responsible person but you can do a pull request for changes any time.

docs.title: Project Layout
docs.text:
The project is organized as follows:

  • docker/: Configuration for the Docker environment.
  • px4/: PX4 Autopilot source code submodule.
  • docs/: Documentation source files (MkDocs).
    • docs/: Markdown content.
    • mkdocs.yml: Site configuration.
  • src/: ROS 2 packages and source code.
    • perception/: Perception modules and algorithms.
    • utils/: Utility packages.
  • launch/: Global launch files for the project (e.g., perception.launch.py).
  • scripts/: Helper scripts for setup and running simulations.
  • sim/: Simulation resources, including Gazebo worlds and models.
  • docker-compose.yaml: Docker Compose definition for services and volumes.

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text:
Page Owner: Leads of the Aeronautics Division

This repo gives us a ready-to-use drone racing environment in Docker. Why Docker? → So everyone works in the same environment, avoiding “it works on my machine” issues.

It bundles:

ROS 2 Humble → our robotics framework

Gazebo (gz) → 3D simulator for drones

PX4 SITL → autopilot software in simulation

MAVROS / MAVSDK → talk between PX4 and ROS

Workspace /ws → where we put our ROS 2 packages

Host OS: Ubuntu/Linux recommended Requires: Docker Engine + Compose v2

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text: Note: after step 3, the container will be running in the background. You can stop it with docker compose down. You can access the documentation at http://localhost:8000.

docs.title: Step 0 — One-time: Set up SSH for GitHub (if you’ve never done this)
docs.text: We need SSH so git clone works smoothly without typing passwords. Follow GitHub’s guide: Follow Github's guide here

docs.title: Step 1 — Clone (with PX4 submodule)
docs.text:
git clone --recurse-submodules git@github.com:ETHRoboticsClub/ETHRC-Drone-Racing.git
cd ETHRC-Drone-Racing
git submodule update --init --recursive

docs.title: Step 2 — Build the Docker image
docs.text: docker compose build

docs.title: Step 2b — Prepare host ROS 2 build/log directories
docs.text:
Run once (or after permission issues) on the host to create .colcon/ros2_ws/{build,install,log} with your user owning them: 

./scripts/prepare_colcon_volumes.sh

docs.title: Step 3 — Start services (enable GUI, start container, open shell)
docs.text:
# Allow container GUI apps to open windows on your desktop (X11)
xhost +local:root
# Start the container (detached) and open a shell inside
docker compose up -d
docker exec -it erc-aeronautics bash

docs.title: Step 4 - Build the whole pipeline
docs.text: colcon build --cmake-args -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release --executor sequential

docs.title: Run the simulation in the container
docs.text:
# Default x500 in the default world
source install/setup.bash
cd /ws/px4/PX4-Autopilot
make clean
make px4_sitl gz_x500_cam

docs.title: Adding Custom Worlds
docs.text:
Place worlds here: 

px4/PX4-Autopilot/Tools/simulation/gz/worlds/

Set which world is loaded in: 

px4/PX4-Autopilot/ROMFS/px4fmu_common/init.d-posix/4022_gz_x500_cam
PX4_GZ_WORLD=<world_name>

docs.title: Command the drone to fly
docs.text: Use Mavsdk API (offboard or action library) or Qgroundcontrol

docs.title: Project Guidelines
docs.text:
Page Owner: Leads of the Aeronautics Division

This document outlines the guidelines for contributing to the ETHRC Drone Racing project, including documentation standards and development workflow.

docs.title: Documentation Guidelines
docs.text: We use MkDocs with the Material for MkDocs theme.

docs.title: Editing Documentation
docs.text:
Documentation source files are located in docs/docs/. They are written in Markdown, this is a really useful guide by Google.

  • Headers: Use # for page titles and ## for section headers.
  • Code Blocks: Use triple backticks (```) for code blocks. Specify the language for syntax highlighting (e.g., ```bash).
  • Images: Place images in docs/docs/images/ and reference them as ![Alt Text](images/filename.png).
  • Admonitions: Use admonitions for notes, warnings, and tips: 
    !!! note
    This is a note.

docs.title: Running Locally
docs.text:
To preview your changes locally, run the following command from the docs/ directory (or root if using the Docker container):

mkdocs serve

The site will be available at http://localhost:8000.

docs.title: Git Workflow
docs.text:
We follow a standard feature-branch workflow:

  1. Create a Branch: Create a new branch for your feature or fix. 
    git checkout -b feature/my-new-feature
  2. Commit Changes: Make your changes and commit them with clear, descriptive messages. 
    git commit -m "Add new flight controller logic"
  3. Push and PR: Push your branch to GitHub and open a Pull Request (PR) against main.
  4. Review and Merge: After review, merge the PR. Delete the branch after merging.

docs.title: Controls
docs.text:
Page Owner: Saad Lahlou

Welcome to the Controls team documentation.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
<<<<<<< HEAD This section contains documentation for the control algorithms and flight stack configuration. ======= This section contains documentation for the control algorithms and the overall flight stack configuration. It describes how control, estimation, and communication components are structured in the codebase and how they interact during flight.

The architecture is designed to be modular, controller-agnostic, and tightly integrated with ROS 2, while relying on MAVSDK for low-level communication with the vehicle.

docs.title: Codebase Architecture
docs.text:
At a high level, the control stack is organized around three main layers:

  1. ROS 2 control interface (drone_control)
  2. Controller implementations (MPC, RL)
  3. Low-level vehicle interface (MAVSDK / PX4)

Each layer has a clearly defined responsibility, allowing controllers to be swapped or extended with minimal changes to the rest of the system.

docs.title: drone_control: ROS 2 Control Interface
docs.text:
The drone_control module is the central ROS 2 interface for flight control.

It acts as the glue between: - The ground station - The perception and state estimation stack - The controller (MPC or RL) - The low-level vehicle interface (MAVSDK)

docs.title: Responsibilities
docs.text:
drone_control is responsible for:

  • Subscribing to ROS 2 topics providing:
  • State estimation (pose, velocity, attitude, etc.)
  • Setpoints and mission-level commands
  • System and control-related signals from the ground station
  • Managing the control logic and execution flow
  • Selecting and running the active controller
  • Publishing low-level control commands to ROS 2 topics

These command topics are then consumed by the MAVSDK client, which forwards them to the drone.

docs.title: Command Path: ROS 2 → MAVSDK → Drone
docs.text:
The control flow is as follows:

  1. State estimation and setpoints are produced by the perception stack and/or ground station and published on ROS 2 topics.
  2. drone_control:
  3. Collects the current state
  4. Passes it to the active controller
  5. Receives actuator-level or rate-level commands
  6. drone_control publishes these commands on a dedicated ROS 2 topic.
  7. MAVSDK subscribes to this topic and:
  8. Converts the commands to MAVSDK offboard messages
  9. Sends them to the drone via MAVLink

This design ensures a clean separation between control logic and vehicle communication.

docs.title: Controller Implementations: MPC and RL
docs.text:
The actual control laws are implemented in separate modules:

  • MPC: Model Predictive Control–based controller
  • RL: Reinforcement Learning–based controller

Each controller: - Consumes the current estimated state - Outputs control commands (e.g. body rates + thrust or per-motor thrust)

Currently, the MPC outputs body rates + collective thrust, (we just realize that MAVSDK can send per-motor thrust), it is planned to change the model to output per-motor thrust.

docs.title: Modularity Goal
docs.text:
A key design goal is to make drone_control fully controller-agnostic.

Any controller that follows the expected interface can be plugged in, without modifying: - MAVSDK integration - ROS 2 communication - Ground station or perception interfaces

At the moment: - The system has been validated and used primarily with MPC - The RL pipeline still requires: - Policy extraction - Runtime inference integration - ROS 2–level interfacing

docs.title: Current Status and Future Work
docs.text:
• MPC is fully integrated and operational
  • RL support is under development
  • Policy loading and inference need to be finalized
  • Interface alignment with drone_control is still required

The existing architecture already supports this extension, and only the controller-specific logic needs to be added.

For detailed information on each controller and their interfaces, please refer to: - MPC - RL - DRONE_CONTROL - MAVSDK

Troubleshooting: For troubleshooting of common problems, check General Control Troubleshooting

docs.title: Drone Control
docs.text: Page Owner: Michalis Papadakis

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This node implements the drone controller that receives the estimated system state and executes pose or trajectory goals via ROS 2 actions.

Important: The node is intented to be controller agnostic, so: 1. multiple controllers can utilize the same interfaces 2. multiple controllers can handle different goals (e.g. LQR for hovering, MPC/RL for trajectory tracking, PID for landing etc)

To achieve this, the node has 2 state flags: active_goal that indicates if the action server serves an action, and hovering_active that indicates if the controller has entered a hovering state, where it stabilizes the current state. When executing a particular goal, the controller stops hovering and uses the controller associated with the particular action.

Note: Currently the controller only supports MPC for hovering, pose and trajectory goals, and needs modifications to support other controllers. The action interface is intented for task-specific controllers, the code needs to be improved for that.

All the parameters are configured in drone_controller_config.yaml

docs.title: Action Interfaces
docs.text: The node exposes the following ROS 2 action servers for goal-based control.

docs.title: Set Pose Goal Action
docs.text:
• Action Name: /drone_set_pose_goal
  • Type: FollowWaypoints
  • Description: Commands the drone to move to a single target pose
  • Behavior:
  • Accepts a pose goal only if currently no other goal is active
  • Disables hovering controller so pose controller can be activated
  • Executes closed-loop control until the target is reached with a specified threshold (specified by the threshold parameter) or the goal is canceled.
  • Finishing the execution, it launches a hovering thread that stabilizes the current state.

docs.title: Set Trajectory Goal Action
docs.text:
• Action Name: /drone_set_trajectory_goal
  • Type: FollowWaypoints
  • Description: Commands the drone to follow a sequence of waypoints (trajectory)
  • Behavior:
  • Accepts a list of waypoints only if currently no other goal is active
  • Disables hovering controller so pose controller can be activated
  • Executes closed-loop control until the target is reached with a specified threshold (specified by the threshold parameter) or the goal is canceled.
  • Finishing the execution, it launches a hovering thread that stabilizes the current state.

The helper nodes: send_pose_goal and send_trajectory_goal showcase the use of the action inteface and its pre-emption capabilities from the CLI and can be used for developement. Their used is shown below However, the GUI is the intented action client.

docs.title: Input Topics
docs.text: This controller node subscribes to the following ROS 2 topics:

docs.title: Drone State
docs.text:
• Topic: specified by state_topic parameter. (Default: drone_state_sim)
    • \drone_state_sim: For getting the state from mavsdk
    • <perception_topic>: For getting the state from perception pipeline
  • Type: std_msgs/msg/Float64MultiArray
  • Description: Current drone state vector (e.g., position, velocity, quaternion, angular velocity)
  • Frequency: sim: 200Hz
  • Queue Size: 10

docs.title: Command Topics
docs.text: The controller node publishes the following ROS 2 topics:

docs.title: AttitudeRate Command
docs.text:
• Topic: specified by attitude_command_topic parameter. (Default: /drone_attitude_cmd)
  • Type: std_msgs/msg/Float64MultiArray
  • Description: Attitude rate command sent to the drone (e.g., roll-rate, pitch-rate, yaw-rate, normalized-thrust). See AttitudeRate
  • Frequency: specified by controller_rate parameter (Default: 100hz)
  • Queue Size: 10

docs.title: Position Command
docs.text:
• Topic: specified by position_command_topic parameter. (Default: drone_position_cmd)
  • Type: std_msgs/msg/Float64MultiArray
  • Description: Position command sent in the earth NED frame. See PositionNedYaw
  • Frequency: specified by controller_rate parameter (Default: 100hz)
  • Queue Size: 10

docs.title: Current Target Pose
docs.text: This is used to visualize the active pose target in rviz and telemetry - Topic: /drone_current_target - Type: geometry_msgs/msg/PoseStamped - Description: Current target pose that the controller is tracking (e.g., active waypoint) - QoS: - Durability: TRANSIENT_LOCAL - Depth: 1 - Frequency: Updated on target changes or during trajectory execution

docs.title: Run the node
docs.text:
1. Run the simulation first: 

    cd ~/ros_ws/px4/PX4-Autopilot && make px4_sitl gz_x500

  2. Run the mpc controller, mavsdk client && plotjuggler visualization 

    ros2 launch drone_control drone_controller.launch.py

  3. You can test the controller from CLI with (this is a placeholder node, since this functionalities will be implemented using GUI):

    Important: Make sure drone is armed. At startup, if one does not give a command, it disarms automatically. One can arm it by: 

    ros2 service call /arm_drone std_srvs/srv/SetBool "{data: true}"

    Position goals: 

    ros2 run drone_control send_pose_goal goal_only -x 0.0 -y 0.0 -z -1.0 -yaw 0.0

    Trajectory goals: 1. Modify the yaml_file 2. Run 

    ros2 run drone_control send_trajectory_goal goal_only

docs.title: MAVSDK
docs.text: Page Owner: Saad Lahlou

docs.title: What is MAVSDK?
docs.text:
MAVSDK (Micro Air Vehicle Software Development Kit) is a high-level, language-agnostic API designed to control and interact with MAVLink-compatible vehicles such as drones and ground robots. It provides an abstraction layer on top of MAVLink, allowing developers to communicate with an autopilot without dealing directly with low-level message handling.

MAVSDK supports multiple programming languages (C++, Python, Swift, Java) and exposes a plugin-based API for telemetry, offboard control, mission handling, parameter access, and system health monitoring.

In practice, MAVSDK is the bridge between PX4 and our code, running on the companion computer.

docs.title: PX4 Autopilot
docs.text:
PX4 is an open-source autopilot system running on the flight controller hardware. It is responsible for estimation, control, safety logic, and actuator outputs, and exposes its interface via MAVLink.

In our stack, we do not rely on PX4’s EKF nor on its internal cascaded PID controllers for nominal operation. State estimation and control are handled externally by our own pipelines (e.g. MPC, RL). However, PX4 remains available as a fallback: its estimator and controllers can be re-enabled if needed for safety, debugging, or recovery.

We chose PX4 because it is:

  • Highly modular and well-structured
  • Supported by a rich ecosystem of tools:
  • Software-In-The-Loop (SITL) with Gazebo
  • Hardware-In-The-Loop (HITL)
  • Backed by a large and active community
  • Fully compatible with MAVSDK

While our long-term goal is to minimize dependence on PX4 for control and estimation, we keep it in the stack to manage low-level flight infrastructure and safety-critical components.

docs.title: MAVLink
docs.text:
MAVLink is a lightweight communication protocol used to exchange messages between:

  • PX4 (flight controller)
  • Companion computers
  • Ground control stations (e.g. QGroundControl)

It defines standardized messages for telemetry, odometry, vehicle state, commands, parameters, and system status. MAVSDK abstracts this protocol and exposes a clean, robust API.

docs.title: MAVSDK in Our Architecture
docs.text:
In our architecture, MAVSDK acts as the bridge between PX4 and our ROS 2-based codebase.

A dedicated MAVSDK client is embedded inside ROS 2, allowing our autonomy, estimation, and control modules to communicate with the flight controller through a unified interface. MAVSDK handles all low-level communication, while our code focuses on high-level logic.

docs.title: Connecting to the Drone
docs.text:
The connection mechanism depends on the execution context:

  • PX4 SITL MAVSDK typically connects over UDP to a simulated PX4 instance (e.g. Gazebo).

  • Real hardware MAVSDK connects over serial (USB/UART) or UDP, depending on the companion computer and flight controller setup.

Once connected, MAVSDK manages system discovery, heartbeats, and link monitoring.

docs.title: Data Flow: PX4 → MAVSDK → ROS 2
docs.text:
Using the MAVSDK API, we retrieve:

  • Estimator outputs and telemetry
  • PX4 odometry (position, velocity, orientation)
  • Vehicle status
  • Arming state
  • Flight mode
  • System health and failsafe status

This data is forwarded to ROS 2 and consumed by higher-level modules.

docs.title: Standard PX4 Control Path
docs.text:
By default, MAVSDK offboard commands rely on PX4’s cascaded PID control architecture. Commands such as body rates and collective thrust are processed by PX4 controllers before being converted into actuator outputs.

This mode is useful for safety and rapid prototyping, but it constrains full control authority.

docs.title: Direct Per-Motor Thrust Control
docs.text:
Our primary objective is to bypass PX4’s internal control loops and directly command the actuators. We therefore support per-motor thrust commands, enabling:

  • Full control authority for MPC or RL policies
  • Independence from PX4’s cascaded PID controllers
  • Clear separation between control logic and hardware interfacing

In this setup, MAVSDK is used purely as a helper for low-level communication and system management, not as a control algorithm.

docs.title: Why We Keep MAVSDK and PX4
docs.text:
Even when bypassing PX4 controllers and estimation, we retain both components because they provide:

  • Robust communication and system management (via MAVSDK)
  • Access to telemetry, status, and safety mechanisms
  • A reliable plan B using PX4’s native estimator and controllers if needed

In the long term, PX4 and MAVSDK may no longer be required, but for now we keep them to manage the interface layer handling low-level interaction with the vehicle.

In summary, MAVSDK is the communication backbone between PX4 and our ROS 2 autonomy stack, while PX4 serves as a modular, tool-rich, and safety-capable platform that we can fall back on when necessary.

docs.title: Model Predictive Control (MPC)
docs.text:
Page Owner: Mattia De Martino, Michalis Papadakis

This section documents the Model Predictive Control (MPC) implementation contained in the mpc folder. The MPC is implemented using CasADi for symbolic modeling and ACADOS for solving the nonlinear optimal control problem (OCP).

The controller computes total thrust and body-rate commands, which are later converted into MAVSDK offboard commands.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The MPC implementation is structured into three main components:

  1. drone_model.py – Drone dynamics and constraints
  2. drone_opt.py – ACADOS optimal control problem and solver
  3. drone_mpc_controller.py – High-level MPC controller interface

The execution flow is:

  • Current state and reference are provided to the MPC controller
  • The optimizer solves a finite-horizon OCP
  • The first control input is extracted
  • The command is converted to a MAVSDK-compatible AttitudeRate

docs.title: Drone Dynamics Model (drone_model.py)
docs.text: This file defines the drone model used by the MPC and exports it in a format compatible with ACADOS.

docs.title: State Definition
docs.text:
The state vector has 13 dimensions:

  • Position p (3): NED frame
  • Velocity v (3): NED frame
  • Quaternion q (4): body → NED
  • Body angular rates w (3)

docs.title: Control Inputs
docs.text:
The control vector has 4 inputs:

  • Total thrust (N)
  • Body rate commands: roll, pitch, yaw (rad/s)

docs.title: Dynamics
docs.text:
The model includes:

  • Position dynamics Position derivative equals velocity.

  • Translational dynamics Thrust is applied in the body frame and rotated to the NED frame using the quaternion. Gravity is applied in the NED frame. An optional drag term is present but set to zero.

  • Quaternion kinematics Quaternion derivative is computed from body angular rates. The quaternion is normalized to avoid numerical drift.

  • Angular rate dynamics Angular rates follow a first-order tracking model: w_dot = (w_cmd - w) / tau_w

docs.title: Physical Parameters and Constraints
docs.text:
The model includes: - Mass and inertia - Maximum thrust derived from motor parameters - Thrust limits - Body rate limits - Bounds on: - Angular rates - Velocity - Position

All constraints are stored and later used by the optimizer.

docs.title: ACADOS Model Export
docs.text:
The model is exported with: - Explicit and implicit dynamics - State and control definitions - Constraint information

This allows direct integration into an ACADOS OCP.

docs.title: MPC Optimizer (drone_opt.py)
docs.text: This file defines and solves the nonlinear OCP using ACADOS.

docs.title: Horizon Setup
docs.text:
• Prediction horizon: T
  • Number of nodes: N

docs.title: Cost Function
docs.text: An external nonlinear cost is used.

docs.title: Stage Cost
docs.text: The stage cost penalizes: - Position error - Velocity error - Quaternion error (Euclidean difference) - Angular rate error - Control effort (thrust deviation from hover and body rates)

docs.title: Terminal Cost
docs.text: The terminal cost penalizes: - Position error - Velocity error - Quaternion error - Angular rate error

docs.title: Parameters and References
docs.text: The reference state is passed as a parameter to the solver. The optimizer supports: - Point-to-point control - Reference trajectory tracking

docs.title: Constraints
docs.text: The optimizer enforces: - Control bounds (thrust and body rates) - State bounds on angular rates - Fixed initial state at the beginning of each solve

docs.title: MPC Solve Step
docs.text:
At each control step: 1. The current state is normalized (quaternion) 2. References are set for all nodes 3. The solver is initialized (with warm start if available) 4. The OCP is solved 5. The first control input is extracted

If the solver fails, an exception is raised and logged.

docs.title: MPC Controller Interface (drone_mpc_controller.py)
docs.text: This file provides the interface between the MPC and the rest of the system.

docs.title: Responsibilities
docs.text: The controller: - Initializes the drone model and optimizer - Receives the current state estimate - Receives a goal position or reference trajectory - Calls the optimizer

docs.title: Control Output
docs.text:
The MPC outputs: - Thrust in Newtons - Body rates in rad/s

These are converted to: - Normalized thrust in [0, 1] - Body rates in degrees per second

The final output is a MAVSDK AttitudeRate command.

docs.title: Error Handling
docs.text: If the optimizer fails: - A safe hover command is returned - Debug information can be logged for analysis

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The MPC module provides: - A physically consistent drone model - A constrained nonlinear MPC formulation - A clear interface for integration with the flight stack

It is currently the main controller implemented in the codebase and serves as the reference control implementation.

docs.title: Reinforcement Learning (RL)
docs.text: Page Owner: Ishaan Jain, Mahmoud El Minawi, Maté Tirpak

docs.title: 1. Compute Requirements (Optional)
docs.text:
If your local machine does not have enough GPU compute, you can request a cloud VM to run training.

Follow the instructions here: https://www.notion.so/Getting-started-with-AWS-and-the-Nvidia-IsaacSim-Workstation-AMI-29cca831cdd380eb9a72c2de794d1ef3

Once the VM is ready (or if you use your own machine), continue with the steps below.

docs.title: 2. Clone the Repository
docs.text:
git clone git@github.com:ETHRoboticsClub/IsaacLab_aeronautics.git
cd IsaacLab_aeronautics

docs.title: 3. Start IsaacLab (Docker-Based Setup)
docs.text:
IsaacLab runs entirely inside Docker. Start the container with:

python docker/container.py start
Then enter the running container: 
python docker/container.py enter
Inside the container, your terminal prompt will look like: 
root@ip-xxx-xx-xx-xxx:/workspace/isaaclab#
This means you are now working inside the IsaacLab environment.

docs.title: 4. Location of the Custom Quadrotor Environment
docs.text:
Our modified quadrotor environment (a copy of the default quadcopter task) is located at: 

source/
    Isaaclab_tasks/
        Isaaclab_tasks/
            direct/
                quadcopter_copy/
Modify files in this folder to change:

  • the policy
  • dynamics
  • task logic
  • observations
  • rewards
  • or any other environment behavior

docs.title: 5. Training the Quadrotor Environment
docs.text:
Inside the container, run: 

python scripts/reinforcement_learning/rsl_rl/train.py \
    --task=Isaac-Quadcopter-Direct-v0-Copy \
    --headless \
    --video \
    --video_length 500 \
    --video_interval 1000

docs.title: Explanation of Flags
docs.text:
Flag Description --task=Isaac-Quadcopter-Direct-v0-Copy Selects the custom quadrotor task you created. --headless Runs training without rendering (faster, required on VMs). --video Enables video recording during training. --video_length 500 Each recorded video clip is 500 simulation steps long. --video_interval 1000 Records a new video every 1000 training iterations.

Videos are saved automatically inside the runs/ directory.

docs.title: 6. Additional Resources
docs.text:
For more details on:

  • environment creation
  • task registration
  • RL integrations
  • logging, debugging, or visualization

refer to the official IsaacLab documentation:

👉 https://isaac-sim.github.io/IsaacLab/

docs.title: 7. Overview of the Current Environment Setup
docs.text: The provided QuadcopterEnvCopy environment is a modified version of the default IsaacLab quadcopter task. It introduces a time-based circular trajectory that the drone must follow, along with small vertical oscillations.

docs.title: What the Drone Is Trained to Do
docs.text:
The quadrotor is trained using reinforcement learning to:

  • Track a moving goal position that follows a circular path around each environment's origin.
  • Maintain stable flight while adjusting thrust and rotational moments.
  • Minimize:
  • linear velocity error
  • angular velocity error
  • distance to the moving goal

docs.title: How the Trajectory Works
docs.text:
Each environment receives: - A unique random phase offset (so not all drones fly in sync), - A circular XY path with adjustable radius and period, - A small vertical oscillation added to the Z position.

The desired trajectory is computed every step and used to generate: - Observations (target position in the quadrotor’s body frame), - Rewards (distance-to-goal mapping, velocity penalties), - Done conditions (crashing or flying too high).

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: In its current form, the drone learns to fly smoothly along a dynamic circular trajectory, staying close to a moving 3D point while maintaining stable and efficient control. This setup is ideal for testing trajectory tracking, stability control, and low-level motor policy behavior.

docs.title: ArUco Pose Estimation
docs.text: Page Owner: Xander Yap & Jules Schmutz

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: We provide an ArUco marker [DICT_5x5_1000] detection system serving as an initial gate detection pipeline and as a fallback ground truth method. The markers have to be physically placed in the environment, subsequently ground truth location and the size of the markers have to be parsed into the system.

docs.title: Input Topics
docs.text: The ArUco pose estimation system subscribes to the following ROS2 topics:

docs.title: Camera Images
docs.text:
• /cam0/image_raw

  • Type: sensor_msgs/msg/Image

  • Description: Raw camera images from a single camera
  • Frequency: Typically 20-30 Hz

docs.title: Output Topics
docs.text: The ArUco pose estimations system publishes the following ROS 2 topics (under namespace /aruco by default):

docs.title: Diagnostic
docs.text:
• /aruco/camera_pose

    • Type: geometry_msgs::msg::PoseStamped
    • Description: Publishes the pose and location of the camera

  • /aruco/drone_pose

    • Type: geometry_msgs::msg::PoseWithCovarianceStamped
    • Description: Publishes the pose and location of the drone

  • /aruco/visualization_markers

    • Type: visualization_msgs::msg::Marker
    • Description: Publishes point cloud markers (for e.g. rviz2) to show the pose and location of the drone

  • /aruco/diagnostics

    • Type: diagnostic_msgs::msg::DiagnosticArray
    • Description: Publishes the values in the terminal

docs.title: Brief explanation
docs.text:
This section provides a short walkthrough and explanation of the detection system:

  1. Configuration: as mentioned in the overview, parse the marker ID, pose, and size into a YAML file in config/.

  2. Detection: we utilize the marker detection library from OpenCV and enhance the performance with Lucas-Kanade optical flow and a smoothening factor.

  3. Visual Update: the borders of the detected markers will be highlighted.

  4. Output: The estimated pose is published as a 6-DoF transform consisting of:

  5. Position: (x, y, z)
  6. Orientation: quaternion (x, y, z, w)

docs.title: Launch ArUco Marker Estimation in Gazebo Simulation
docs.text: ros2 launch aruco_pose_estimation aruco_pose_estimation.launch.py

docs.title: Extended Kalman Filter (EKF)
docs.text: Page Owner: Oliver Calvet

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: The EKF package provides sensor fusion for drone state estimation by leveraging the Robot Localization package's Extended Kalman Filter implementation. The filter fuses visual-inertial odometry (VIO) from OpenVINS with absolute pose measurements from ArUco marker detection to produce a robust, high-frequency state estimate. The current implementation uses the standard robot_localization package without drone-specific model adaptations.

docs.title: Input Topics
docs.text: The EKF system subscribes to the following ROS 2 topics. Orientation data arrives as quaternions but is internally converted to roll, pitch, yaw (RPY) for the filter's 15-dimensional state vector: [x, y, z, roll, pitch, yaw, vx, vy, vz, vroll, vpitch, vyaw, ax, ay, az].

docs.title: VIO Odometry
docs.text:
• Topic: /ov_msckf/odomimu
  • Type: nav_msgs/msg/Odometry
  • Description: Odometry from OpenVINS containing pose (position + orientation) and velocity estimates
  • Used for Update: x, y, z, roll, pitch, yaw, vx, vy, vz, vroll, vpitch, vyaw

docs.title: ArUco Pose
docs.text:
• Topic: /aruco/drone_pose
  • Type: geometry_msgs/msg/PoseWithCovarianceStamped
  • Description: Absolute pose measurements from ArUco marker detection
  • Used for Update: x, y, z, roll, pitch, yaw

docs.title: Control Input (Optional)
docs.text:
• Topic: /control/command (remapped from cmd_vel)
  • Type: geometry_msgs/msg/Twist
  • Description: Velocity commands used for motion prediction (currently disabled)

docs.title: Output Topics
docs.text: The EKF system publishes the following ROS 2 topics:

docs.title: Fused Odometry
docs.text:
• /ekf/odometry
  • Type: nav_msgs/msg/Odometry
  • Description: Fused state estimate containing pose and velocity with covariances
  • Frequency: 100 Hz (configurable via frequency parameter)

docs.title: Acceleration
docs.text:
• /accel/filtered
  • Type: geometry_msgs/msg/AccelWithCovarianceStamped
  • Description: Estimated linear acceleration

docs.title: Transforms (TF)
docs.text:
• /tf
  • Description: Transform from world frame to base_link frame via odom frame
  • Frequency: 100 Hz

docs.title: Brief Explanation
docs.text:
The sensor fusion pipeline works as follows:

  1. Prediction Step: The filter propagates the state estimate forward in time using a constant-velocity motion model. The prediction runs at 100 Hz to maintain smooth state estimates.

  2. VIO Update: When odometry messages arrive from OpenVINS (/ov_msckf/odomimu), the filter incorporates full pose and velocity information (x, y, z, roll, pitch, yaw, vx, vy, vz, vroll, vpitch, vyaw) to update the state estimate.

  3. Vision Update: Absolute pose measurements from ArUco marker detection (/aruco/drone_pose) provide global corrections to prevent drift. Only pose states (x, y, z, roll, pitch, yaw) are fused from this source.

  4. Delayed Measurement Handling: The filter maintains a 0.5-second state history buffer (smooth_lagged_data: true) to properly handle out-of-order or delayed sensor measurements.

  5. Output: The fused state estimate is published as odometry and TF transforms for use by other modules.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
The filter parameters are configured in config/rl_ekf.yaml. Key settings include:

Parameter Value Description frequency 100.0 Hz Filter update rate sensor_timeout 0.1 s Timeout before sensor is considered stale publish_tf true Publish TF transforms two_d_mode false Full 3D state estimation history_length 0.5 s State history for delayed measurements

docs.title: Frame Configuration
docs.text:
Frame Value Description map_frame world Global fixed reference frame for the environment odom_frame odom Continuous odometry frame (can drift over time) base_link_frame base_link Frame rigidly attached to the drone body world_frame world Reference frame for filter operation

Setting world_frame: world (same as map_frame) configures the filter to operate in the global map frame. This is required because we fuse absolute pose measurements from ArUco markers, which provide global corrections and eliminate drift. If world_frame were set to odom, the filter would only output continuous odometry without incorporating these global corrections.

docs.title: Launch EKF in Gazebo Simulation
docs.text:
ros2 launch ekf rl_ekf.launch.xml

This starts the robot_localization EKF node with fused odometry published on /ekf/odometry.

docs.title: Visual Inertial Odometry (VIO)
docs.text: Page Owner: Giacomo Piatelli

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: OpenVINS is a state-of-the-art filter-based visual-inertial odometry system that estimates the 6-DOF pose (position and orientation) and velocity of the drone by fusing camera images with IMU measurements. The system uses an Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) with Multi-State Constraint Kalman Filter (MSCKF) formulation to efficiently track visual features and estimate the state without directly estimating feature positions in the filter state.

docs.title: Input Topics
docs.text: The VIO system subscribes to the following ROS 2 topics:

docs.title: IMU Data
docs.text:
• Topic: /imu0 (default, configurable via topic_imu parameter)
  • Type: sensor_msgs/msg/Imu
  • Description: IMU measurements containing linear acceleration and angular velocity
  • Frequency: Typically 200-400 Hz

docs.title: Camera Images
docs.text:
• Monocular Mode:
  • Topic: /cam0/image_raw (default, configurable via topic_camera0 parameter)
  • Type: sensor_msgs/msg/Image
  • Description: Raw camera images from a single camera

  • Frequency: Typically 20-30 Hz

  • Stereo Mode:

  • Topics: /cam0/image_raw and /cam1/image_raw (default, configurable)
  • Type: sensor_msgs/msg/Image
  • Description: Synchronized stereo image pairs
  • Frequency: Typically 20-30 Hz (synchronized)

docs.title: Output Topics
docs.text: The VIO system publishes the following ROS 2 topics (under namespace /ov_msckf by default):

docs.title: Pose and Odometry
docs.text:
• /ov_msckf/poseimu
  • Type: geometry_msgs/msg/PoseWithCovarianceStamped
  • Description: Current pose estimate (position + orientation) with covariance

  • Frequency: ~20 Hz (tracking frequency, configurable via track_frequency parameter)

  • /ov_msckf/odomimu

  • Type: nav_msgs/msg/Odometry
  • Description: High-frequency odometry message containing pose, velocity, and covariances

  • Frequency: Up to IMU rate (200-400 Hz) for high-frequency pose estimates

  • /ov_msckf/pathimu

  • Type: nav_msgs/msg/Path
  • Description: Historical trajectory path
  • Frequency: ~20 Hz

docs.title: Visual Features
docs.text:
• /ov_msckf/points_msckf
  • Type: sensor_msgs/msg/PointCloud2
  • Description: 3D point cloud of MSCKF tracked features

  • Frequency: ~20 Hz

  • /ov_msckf/points_slam

  • Type: sensor_msgs/msg/PointCloud2
  • Description: 3D point cloud of SLAM features (features in state vector)

  • Frequency: ~20 Hz

  • /ov_msckf/trackhist

  • Type: sensor_msgs/msg/Image
  • Description: Visualization image showing tracked features
  • Frequency: 20 Hz

docs.title: Transforms (TF)
docs.text:
• /tf
  • Description: Transform from global frame to imu frame, and from imu to cam0, cam1, etc.
  • Frequency: ~20 Hz

docs.title: Brief Explanation
docs.text:
The VIO pipeline works as follows:

  1. Feature Extraction & Tracking: Visual features are detected and tracked across consecutive camera frames using KLT (Kanade-Lucas-Tomasi) tracking.

  2. IMU Propagation: Between camera frames, the IMU measurements are integrated to propagate the state estimate forward in time, providing high-frequency motion estimates.

  3. Visual Update: When new camera frames arrive, the tracked features are used to update the state estimate. The MSCKF formulation allows using visual constraints without explicitly estimating 3D feature positions in the filter state, making it computationally efficient.

  4. State Estimation: The EKF maintains estimates of:

  5. Pose (position and orientation)
  6. Velocity
  7. IMU biases
  8. Camera-IMU calibration (extrinsics)

  9. Camera intrinsics (if enabled)

  10. Output: The estimated pose, velocity, and trajectory are published to ROS 2 topics for use by other modules.

docs.title: Launch OpenVINS in Gazebo Simulation
docs.text:
ros2 launch ov_msckf subscribe.launch.py config:=gazebo_sim use_stereo:=false config_path:=/home/drone_dev/ros_ws/src/open_vins/config/gazebo_sim/estimator_config.yaml use_stereo:=false max_cameras:=1
Important to enforce the use stereo and max cameras parameter otherwise it give segemntation fault error

docs.title: Debug Segemntation Error
docs.text:
In case of segmentation error to be able to debug add the following line in the ov_msckf/launch/subscribe.launch.py file:

    node1 = Node(
        package="ov_msckf",
        executable="run_subscribe_msckf",
        condition=IfCondition(LaunchConfiguration("ov_enable")),
        namespace=LaunchConfiguration("namespace"),
        output='screen',
        prefix=['gdb -ex run -ex "bt full" -ex quit --args'], # ADD THIS LINE
        parameters=[
            {"verbosity": LaunchConfiguration("verbosity")},
            {"use_stereo": ParameterValue(LaunchConfiguration("use_stereo"), value_type=bool)},
            {"max_cameras": ParameterValue(LaunchConfiguration("max_cameras"), value_type=int)},
            {"save_total_state": ParameterValue(LaunchConfiguration("save_total_state"), value_type=bool)},
            {"config_path": config_path},
            {"record_timing_information": ParameterValue(LaunchConfiguration("dotime"), value_type=bool)},
            {"record_timing_filepath": LaunchConfiguration("path_time")},
        ],
    )

This way we are going to enable gdb, which give us the possibility of trace back which function call lead to the segemntatiton fault
